title: Probiotic and microbial modulation of polyamine production: an emerging avenue for neuroprotection in neurodegenerative disorders

sections.abstract:
Neurodegenerative disorders are an Critical worldwide issue, characterized by progressive neuronal loss and cognitive decline with limited effective therapies. A central problem in these conditions is chronic neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and disrupted cellular homeostasis. Polyamines, such as putrescine, spermidine, and spermine—small molecules—play vital roles in maintaining neuronal function, regulating autophagy, and protecting against cellular stress. Notably, spermidine-induced autophagy has emerged as a key mechanism linking polyamine metabolism to neuronal longevity and cognitive resilience. Recent studies highlight that probiotics and specific gut microbes can effectively modulate host polyamine production through the gut-brain axis, influencing neural health. This microbial modulation has been shown to restore polyamine balance, enhance antioxidant defenses, and reduce neuroinflammatory responses. Targeting microbiota-driven polyamine synthesis is emerging as a promising, non-invasive approach for neuroprotection. This review consolidates the current understanding of polyamine biology and microbial influences, highlighting their therapeutic potential. Exploring these interactions offers new avenues for innovation in combatting neurodegenerative disorders.

Keywords: Polyamines, Probiotics, Gut–brain axis, Neuroprotection, Neurodegenerative disorders, Microbial modulation, Oxidative stress, Neuroinflammation, Spermidine, Autophagy
sections.introduction:
Neurodegenerative disorders (NDs) form a diverse group of chronic and progressive conditions characterized by selective neuronal loss in specific regions of the central nervous system. This degeneration disrupts neural circuitry and presents clinically as cognitive deficits, motor abnormalities, and behavioral disturbances. Common disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), Huntington’s disease (HD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) share core molecular features including oxidative stress, aberrant protein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and sustained neuroinflammation, all of which drive irreversible neuronal damage (Soto and Pritzkow 2018 ).

Polyamines—particularly putrescine, spermidine, and spermine—have gained prominence as intrinsic modulators of neuronal survival. These polycationic molecules regulate nucleic acid structure, ion channel activity, synaptic signaling, and cellular stress responses. Evidence indicates that polyamines protect neurons by buffering oxidative stress, enhancing synaptic plasticity, and suppressing neuroinflammatory pathways, positioning them as promising neuroprotective candidates in NDs (Minois 2014 ).

Parallel to these molecular insights, the microbiota–gut–brain axis (GBA) has emerged as an influential regulatory network connecting gut microbial activity with brain physiology. Through metabolic, immune, endocrine, and neural pathways, gut microbes influence neuroinflammation, blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability, and neurotransmitter synthesis. Microbial dysbiosis has been implicated in AD, PD, and other NDs, indicating that microbiome modulation may offer a viable route for modifying disease progression (Dinan and Cryan 2017a ).

Polyamines are deeply integrated into this axis: they are synthesized both by host tissues and by gut bacteria. Within the brain, their levels are tightly regulated through balanced biosynthesis, degradation, and transport. Dysregulated polyamine metabolism—observed in AD and PD—has been linked to excessive oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and mitochondrial dysfunction (Xu et al. 2016 ).However, polyamine concentrations in MOST tissues decline with aging. Taken together, understanding polyamine biology within the broader microbiota–gut–brain framework may reveal new therapeutic opportunities for neurodegenerative disease management.
sections.conclusion:
Polyamines play a vital role in sustaining neuronal resilience, synaptic integrity, and overall brain homeostasis by influencing antioxidative defenses, autophagy, mitochondrial stability, and neuroplasticity. Growing scientific evidence places the gut–microbe–polyamine axis at the center of this regulatory network, demonstrating how microbial metabolism can shape brain polyamine availability and, in turn, influence neural health. Probiotic genera such as Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and E. coli are increasingly recognized for their ability to elevate spermidine and spermine levels, thereby activating key protective pathways—including Nrf2, mTOR, and sirtuins. Through these mechanisms, gut-derived polyamines can reduce oxidative stress and neuroinflammation while supporting mitochondrial efficiency and autophagic balance—processes that are typically compromised in neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases.

Insights from the reviewed literature further indicate that strategic modulation of this gut–brain axis through targeted probiotics, microbiome engineering, and personalized nutrition may offer a promising, biologically guided approach to neuroprotection. This integrating of microbial polyamine production with host pathway is crucial for neuronal survival; this framework highlights a potential avenue for advancing interventions, aimed at enhancing long-term brain health and cognitive resilience.
